sources.title: Thomas Joshua Cooper – Overview, Ingleby Gallery Edinburgh
sources.excerpt: Like artists such as Richard Long, and Hamish Fulton, Cooper is a traveller, a nomadic artist whose extraordinary photographs are made in series at significant points around the globe, most often at its extremities. The capturing of any one image can involve days, weeks and months of preparation and arduous travel.

sources.title: Thomas Joshua Cooper – Overview, Ingleby Gallery Edinburgh
sources.excerpt: The locations are found on a map, tracked down and then photographed, each place the subject of a single negative made with a weighty antique field camera.

sources.title: Dana Macfarlane: Thomas Joshua Cooper: ‘The World’s Edge …’ – The Drouth (Rezension)
sources.excerpt: He rejects conventional language for photographing: he does not ‘shoot’ or ‘take’ photographs, preferring to think of his practice as a giving back, an offering.

sources.title: Thomas Joshua Cooper: The World’s Edge – Artist Audio Commentary, LACMA (2019/20; Transkripte)
sources.excerpt: On view from September 22, 2019 to January 26th, 2020 in the Resnick Pavilion, the exhibition comprises 140 works, showcasing Cooper’s The World’s Edge—The Atlas of Emptiness and Extremity , a project to chart the Atlantic basin at its most extreme northern, southern, eastern, and western points that he began in 1987.

sources.title: Thomas Joshua Cooper – Overview, Ingleby Gallery Edinburgh
sources.excerpt: Over 32 years Cooper voyaged to the cardinal points of the continents fringing the Atlantic Basin, charting from pole to pole, and making photographs out to horizonless seas and over apparently limitless landscapes.

sources.title: Thomas Joshua Cooper – Overview, Ingleby Gallery Edinburgh
sources.excerpt: They are meditative, almost philosophical images, exquisitely printed by the artist in the 19th century manner with layers of silver and gold chloride.

sources.excerpt: Darüber hinaus verbindet der Künstler sein Wissen und die Beherrschung alter Techniken (Aufnahmen mit der Fachkamera, Heliogravur, Kolorierung von Schwarz-Weiß-Vorlagen) mit den neuesten digitalen Technologien – digitale Aufnahme, künstliche Intelligenz und sogar noch nie dagewesene Verfahren.

sources.title: Elger Esser: Sky and Sand – Flowers Gallery London (Ausstellungstext, 2025)
sources.excerpt: Continuing Esser’s lifelong exploration of the landscape genre, Sky and Sand delves into the poetic interplay between history, memory, and topography, inviting viewers into a meditative world that reflects Esser’s deep connection to France, a country he describes as carrying "history in its landscape like no other."

sources.title: Biography and CV – michaellight.net
sources.excerpt: For the last eighteen years, Light has aerially photographed over settled and unsettled areas of American space, pursuing themes of mapping, vertigo, human impact on the land, and various aspects of geologic time and the sublime. A private pilot and Guggenheim Fellow in photography, he is currently working on an extended aerial survey of the arid Western states.

sources.title: Geoff Manaugh: Spatial Delirium: An Interview with Michael Light – BLDGBLOG (Oktober 2013)
sources.excerpt: An artist widely known for his aerial work, Light flies the trip himself in a small airplane, usually departing very early in the morning, near dawn, before the turbulence builds up.

sources.excerpt: My work aims to look at the consequences and limitations of that human power carefully in the context of beauty and terror—the fundamentals of the classical landscape sublime—as well as attempt to channel and transcribe some of the power inherent in the many and almost infinite worlds that are not us.

sources.title: Info / Bio – davidmaisel.com
sources.excerpt: His in-depth photographic series and video installations address the psychological and environmental impact of landscapes radically transformed by mineral extraction, natural resource reclamation, desertification, and military weapons testing.

sources.title: Info / Bio – davidmaisel.com
sources.excerpt: His images describe a world wholly remade by human activity; although visually resplendent, they are also spatially ambiguous and destabilizing, with aspects of beauty, fascination, and horror in equal measure.

sources.title: Diana Gaston: David Maisel: The Lake Project – Aperture 172 (Nachdruck auf davidmaisel.com)
sources.excerpt: The early thinking for this series actually began during his undergraduate work at Princeton, when he accompanied his photography professor Emmet Gowin on flights over Mount Saint Helens and the heavily logged forests of the Pacific Northwest.

sources.title: The Lake Project – davidmaisel.com (Projekttext)
sources.excerpt: The Lake Project comprises images from Owens Lake, the site of a formerly 200 square-mile lake in California on the eastern side of the Sierra Mountains. Beginning in 1913, the Owens River was diverted into the Owens Valley Aqueduct, to bring water to the fledgling desert city of Los Angeles.

sources.title: The Lake Project – davidmaisel.com (Projekttext)
sources.excerpt: Viewed from the air, vestiges of the lake appear as a river of blood, a microchip, a bisected vein, or a galaxy’s map. It is this contemporary version of the sublime that Maisel finds find compelling– a strange beauty born of environmental degradation.

sources.title: The Lake Project – davidmaisel.com (Projekttext)
sources.excerpt: Maisel initially worked at Owens Lake making aerial images of this surreal landscape from 2001-2002. He returned to Owens Lake in 2015 to make new images and to see how the intervening years had brought additional layers of human intervention to the lakebed.

sources.title: Diana Gaston: David Maisel: The Lake Project – Aperture 172 (Nachdruck auf davidmaisel.com)
sources.excerpt: It was the unusual pink glow of the lakebed that caught David Maisel’s attention when he drove through Owens Valley on a return trip to the San Francisco Bay Area.

sources.title: Diana Gaston: David Maisel: The Lake Project – Aperture 172 (Nachdruck auf davidmaisel.com)
sources.excerpt: The ground is bleeding. A red river cuts a path through a bleached valley, winding toward a lake that is no longer there. Seen from the air, the river and its dry terminus appear otherworldly.
sources.author: Diana Gaston

sources.title: David Maisel: Report from the Lake – Essay des Fotografen (davidmaisel.com)

sources.excerpt: Nor do his numbered titles offer any information beyond a rigorous cataloguing system of his own making. As engaged as he is in the surrounding issues, Maisel is not attempting to make literal records of environmental destruction. Rather, he seeks a distance that scrambles a conventional reading of the landscape.

sources.title: Diana Gaston: David Maisel: The Lake Project – Aperture 172 (Nachdruck auf davidmaisel.com)
sources.excerpt: With each succeeding layer of intervention the landscape becomes more and more complex, as previous scars are covered over, irrigation pools expand into an authoritative grid system, and the colors on the ground are artificially buffered.

sources.title: About – tomhegen.com
sources.excerpt: My name is Tom Hegen, I work as a Photographer and Designer in Munich, Germany. I focus on aerial photography projects that show impact of human presence on earth. As a photographer I am interested in the relationship between man and nature. In my aerial photography I focus on landscapes that have been heavily transformed by human intervention.

sources.title: Will Higginbotham: Tom Hegen – photographing humanity’s impact on Earth – Port Magazine (Interview)
sources.excerpt: I always felt drawn to landscape photography and spent a long time trying to find those classic landscape image compositions. I always encountered elements like power lines, roads or buildings that were nasty in the picture though. At that time, I started to question the term landscape photography and why I was focused on a composition that tried to pretend to be part of some sort of ‘perfect world’ that didn’t really exist. So I started to focus on man-made landscapes and tried to find visual beauty in them.

sources.title: Will Higginbotham: Tom Hegen – photographing humanity’s impact on Earth – Port Magazine (Interview)
sources.excerpt: I studied communication design. My eye is trained for composition, colour and shapes. The graphic quality of landscapes that comes with the overview perspective is quite unique. I’m still thinking and working as a graphic designer but solely with the medium of photography.

sources.title: Tom Hegen’s aerial photography – CNN Style (Voice Memo, Telefoninterview)
sources.excerpt: Hunting for locations using Google Earth, and ensuring that weather conditions are suitable for flying, Hegen depicts aerial photography as an art grounded in painstaking preparation.

sources.title: The Lithium Series I – tomhegen.com (Projekttext)
sources.excerpt: More than 50% of the worlds lithium resources occur in South America, in the lithium Triangle of Bolivia, Chile and Argentina. The Salar de Atacama salt flats in northern Chile contain more than a quarter of the world's lithium supplies. The biggest lithium evaporation production site globally is even visible from space.

sources.title: The Lithium Series I – tomhegen.com (Projekttext)
sources.excerpt: Brine, rich in lithium from more than 100 meters underneath the salt flats, is pumped into huge pools. Sun evaporates the brine and the concentration of lithium increases

sources.title: The Lithium Series I – tomhegen.com (Projekttext)
sources.excerpt: As we are slowly moving towards a world of sustainable energy, replacing fossil fuels with clean energy causes a new spiral of human impact on the environment.

sources.title: Will Higginbotham: Tom Hegen – photographing humanity’s impact on Earth – Port Magazine (Interview)
sources.excerpt: The distance view shows the dimensions of human impact on the earth and puts our activities in the context of the surrounding landscape.
sources.author: Tom Hegen

sources.title: Will Higginbotham: Tom Hegen – photographing humanity’s impact on Earth – Port Magazine (Interview)
sources.excerpt: German photographer, Tom Hegen, has made a name for himself as a documentarian of the Anthropocene – the current geological age characterised by the impacts of humans on climate and environment.
sources.author: Will Higginbotham (Port Magazine)

sources.title: Tom Hegen’s aerial photography – CNN Style (Voice Memo, Telefoninterview)
sources.excerpt: “I use abstraction and aestheticization to get the viewer’s attention,” the German photographer said in a phone interview. “When first looking at the photos I (want people to) think, ‘wow this is really stunning and beautiful.’ But I hope that, on second glance, they wonder what they’re looking at, and why it looks the way it does.”
sources.author: Tom Hegen

sources.title: Will Higginbotham: Tom Hegen – photographing humanity’s impact on Earth – Port Magazine (Interview)
sources.excerpt: My images possess a great level of abstraction and with a graphical approach. Some images will take time to decode to understand what you are looking at. This adds a fundamental level to it as the audience has to interact with the image and build a relationship with what they see.
sources.author: Tom Hegen

sources.title: Tom Hegen’s aerial photography – CNN Style (Voice Memo, Telefoninterview)
sources.excerpt: By pointing the camera directly down at the Earth, the images appear completely flat, giving them a surreal aesthetic quality.
sources.author: CNN Style

sources.title: Zong Chen, Ding Yining: How China Became One American Photographer’s Muse – Sixth Tone (12. April 2018, Interview)
sources.excerpt: My subject, I always tell everybody, is landscape as culture. None of my photographs are just about nature. I feel like you have to step back and include more for me, to make myself interested.

sources.title: Zong Chen, Ding Yining: How China Became One American Photographer’s Muse – Sixth Tone (12. April 2018, Interview)
sources.excerpt: When I was a young student, I had to take a class and use a big camera on a tripod, and the day I did that, I felt like my life changed. I no longer had to quickly move around with the small camera — it’s on the tripod, I can set it up, I can walk around, I can carry it over my shoulder, but I can pause and look at the landscape.

sources.title: Zong Chen, Ding Yining: How China Became One American Photographer’s Muse – Sixth Tone (12. April 2018, Interview)
sources.excerpt: I might go to a place and do absolutely no work, because I don’t really know where to begin. But then I keep going back until I become familiar enough to have something to say that’s my own.

sources.title: Lois Conner: 1984 – M97 Gallery Shanghai (Ausstellungstext)
sources.excerpt: “The people in my landscapes are just as important as the landscapes themselves ... Without them there is no context, scale, or connection to place. Often they are the reason that I am making the photograph.”

sources.title: Geremie R. Barmé: 顛倒 Downside Up — the art of Lois Conner – China Heritage (20. April 2017; Katalogessay zur Ausstellung in Beijing, mit Text von Xu Zhiyuan)
sources.excerpt: Lois Conner uses a banquet camera, a modern version of a nineteenth-century camera employed by photographers to make pictures of people massed together at such occasions as banquets because of its breadth of vision. It allowed for an elongated frame that could eliminate the distractions of the ceiling and the floor.

sources.title: Lois Conner: 1984 – M97 Gallery Shanghai (Ausstellungstext)
sources.excerpt: With a Guggenheim Fellowship, she left her work at the United Nations in New York to explore the Chinese landscape of Guangxi province using her 7"x17” panoramic camera. The elongated format of her photographs are similar to classical scroll painting and cinematic form.

sources.title: Geremie R. Barmé: 顛倒 Downside Up — the art of Lois Conner – China Heritage (20. April 2017; Katalogessay zur Ausstellung in Beijing, mit Text von Xu Zhiyuan)
sources.excerpt: She has travelled from south to north and back again numerous times as she weaves the worlds of China — modern and traditional, natural and manmade — into an ever-growing body of work that embraces the past, constantly touches on the present, and addresses itself to the future.

sources.title: Zong Chen, Ding Yining: How China Became One American Photographer’s Muse – Sixth Tone (12. April 2018, Interview)
sources.excerpt: (Vertical image: ‘Colossal Buddha,’ taken in Leshan, Sichuan province, 1986. Courtesy of Lois Conner)

sources.title: Geremie R. Barmé: 顛倒 Downside Up — the art of Lois Conner – China Heritage (20. April 2017; Katalogessay zur Ausstellung in Beijing, mit Text von Xu Zhiyuan)
sources.excerpt: First drawn to this format as an arts student at Yale University after she studied the landscape scroll paintings of the Ming dynasty, Conner has been using the format of the panoramic camera to pursue her work in China since 1984. The vistas embraced by the banquet camera allow her to ‘unfurl the landscape’ in a manner suggested by the scroll paintings.
sources.author: Geremie R. Barmé

sources.title: Geremie R. Barmé: 顛倒 Downside Up — the art of Lois Conner – China Heritage (20. April 2017; Katalogessay zur Ausstellung in Beijing, mit Text von Xu Zhiyuan)
sources.excerpt: Here, hidden under the cloth, everything that to the causal eye appears as upright and quotidian is inverted, all that is left-to-right becomes right-to-left. It is the world on the down low.
sources.author: Geremie R. Barmé

sources.title: Lois Conner, Yangshuo, China, 1985 – The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art (Objektseite mit Ausstellungstext)
sources.excerpt: To make this unique landscape view, Lois Conner used a banquet camera, which produces a panoramic negative. The orientation of the landscape evokes parallels with Chinese scroll painting. This is a platinum print, which is characterized by matte surfaces and tonal nuance.

sources.title: About – victoriasambunaris.com
sources.excerpt: For over 25 years, Victoria Sambunaris has structured her life around a photographic journey traversing the American landscape. Equipped with a 5x7 inch field camera, film, a video camera and research material, she crosses the country alone by car for several months per year.

sources.title: Jessica Hays im Gespräch mit Victoria Sambunaris – Lenscratch (Photographers on Photographers)
sources.excerpt: The work is project based and researched in advance. Once I arrive at my destination, I begin by exploring the area, talking to locals, and absorbing information about the place. Of course, chance, luck and the unexpected always factor into the work.

sources.title: Corinne Rose: Viewer’s Guide zu ‚Victoria Sambunaris: Taxonomy of a Landscape‘ – Museum of Contemporary Photography Chicago (2013), PDF
sources.excerpt: She says that she spends much of her time scouting the locations she shoots and uses a medium format camera to create photographic sketches of locations she is interested in photographing.

sources.title: Jessica Hays im Gespräch mit Victoria Sambunaris – Lenscratch (Photographers on Photographers)
sources.excerpt: I see these places more clearly after the distance and the time away.

projects.title: Untitled – Fahrten durch die amerikanische Landschaft (Auswahl 2001–2012)

sources.title: Victoria Sambunaris: Taxonomy of a Landscape – Ausstellungsblatt, Museum of Contemporary Photography Chicago (2013), PDF
sources.excerpt: For more than a decade, Victoria Sambunaris (American, born 1964) has traversed the United States equipped with a five-by-seven wooden field camera and sheets of color negative film. Covering seemingly every road and freeway between the coasts and beyond, she has captured the vast American landscape and terrain, and its intersection with civilization.

sources.title: Victoria Sambunaris: Taxonomy of a Landscape – Ausstellungsblatt, Museum of Contemporary Photography Chicago (2013), PDF
sources.excerpt: Sambunaris photographs the landscape as a document and metaphor for the American experience, bringing into view with photographic precision the vast, open-ended mystery and unease of a country where human intervention and natural beauty inspire wonder in equal measure.

sources.title: About – victoriasambunaris.com
sources.excerpt: Her large-scale photographs document the continuing transformation of the American landscape with specific attention given to expanding political, technological and industrial interventions.

images.title: Untitled, Red containers stacked, Newark, New Jersey

sources.title: Corinne Rose: Viewer’s Guide zu ‚Victoria Sambunaris: Taxonomy of a Landscape‘ – Museum of Contemporary Photography Chicago (2013), PDF
sources.excerpt: From 2000-2002 she created more minimal works that focused on the presence of trains and trucks—vehicles that transport the products of American consumption—in the landscape.
sources.author: Corinne Rose (MoCP)

sources.title: Victoria Sambunaris: Taxonomy of a Landscape – Ausstellungsblatt, Museum of Contemporary Photography Chicago (2013), PDF
sources.excerpt: As she explains, “It is the anomalies of an ordinary landscape that have become the locus of my work: massive warehousing, infinite distribution facilities, and systematized shipping terminals. These numerous paradigmatic structures, I sense, portend the future of landscape and our relationship to it.”
sources.author: Victoria Sambunaris

sources.title: Corinne Rose: Viewer’s Guide zu ‚Victoria Sambunaris: Taxonomy of a Landscape‘ – Museum of Contemporary Photography Chicago (2013), PDF
sources.excerpt: Since creating that work, Sambunaris has continued to photograph the American landscape, but has pulled further back so that evidence of human presence can often be seen, but the land itself dominates most of the frame.
sources.author: Corinne Rose (MoCP)

sources.title: Corinne Rose: Viewer’s Guide zu ‚Victoria Sambunaris: Taxonomy of a Landscape‘ – Museum of Contemporary Photography Chicago (2013), PDF
sources.excerpt: In 2007-08 Sambunaris traveled and photographed along Interstate 80, a main artery of travel and commerce that roughly follows historic routes west and bisects the US from Teaneck, New Jersey to San Francisco, California, connecting many points of cultural and geographic interest along the way.
sources.author: Corinne Rose (MoCP)

sources.title: Corinne Rose: Viewer’s Guide zu ‚Victoria Sambunaris: Taxonomy of a Landscape‘ – Museum of Contemporary Photography Chicago (2013), PDF
sources.excerpt: The consistency in the color and mood of her images is in part due to her consistent use of light. Sambunaris says that she might wait as much as two weeks for for the weather to change to provide the neutral and diffused light she prefers for her work.

sources.title: About – lauramcphee.com
sources.excerpt: She is noted for her stunning large-scale landscapes and portraits of the people who live and work in them. She is currently working in the desert west of the United States where she is chronicling visual stories about time, both geologic and human.

sources.title: “River of No Return” by Photographer Laura McPhee – Booooooom (14. März 2023)
sources.excerpt: “Photography is, of course, a form of preservation, an attempt to distill and to keep. Using 19th-century technology in the 21st, I attempt to slow time and open a space for both contemporary facts and imagination.”

sources.title: “River of No Return” by Photographer Laura McPhee – Booooooom (14. März 2023)
sources.excerpt: “The work is both personal and political, as it takes in the conflicts over land use and considers the possible futures of a landscape we believe to be quintessentially American,” she explains.

sources.excerpt: Collectively, the pictures evoke contemplation of how we use the earth and to what ends.

sources.excerpt: For a number of years, photographer Laura McPhee has been working on Desert Chronicle, a project inspired by her great-grandmother’s work as an itinerant schoolteacher in Nevada, traveling with her two daughters from town to town to educate the children of miners and ranchers.

sources.excerpt: “Desert Chronicle” is a working title for photographs that grew out of her “River of No Return” and “Guardians of Solitude” series.
